## Scenario

The manager of De Hoop Nature Reserve has asked for help mapping wetlands in the reserve. The existing map does not indicate any mountain seep wetlands on Potberg, but these small wetlands are typically important for biodiversity conservation, providing hydrological refugia that support species that may otherwise not be able to survive in the prevailing climate.

---

## What is a seep?

```{r echo = F, fig.align = 'center', out.width = '60%', fig.cap = "(from Ollis et al 2012, SANBI)"}
knitr::include_graphics("images/wetlands_ollis2012SANBI.png")
```

"Seeps are characterised by their association with geological formations (lithologies) and topographic positions that either cause groundwater to discharge to the land surface or rain-derived water to ‘seep’ down-slope as subsurface interflow."

---

## Why are seeps important?

<br>

Seeps provide hydrological refugia that support species that may otherwise not be able to survive in the prevailing climate [(McLaughlin et al. 2017)](https://doi.org/10.1111/gcb.13629).

<br>

Hydric habitats contribute greatly to the richness of the Cape Fynbos Flora [(van Blerk et al. 2025)](https://doi.org/10.1111/ddi.13962).

<br>

Groundwater dependent ecosystems (including seeps) are particularly vulnerable to invasive alien species and groundwater abstraction for human use [(Slingsby 2018)](https://groundup.org.za/article/rush-drill-water-could-threaten-our-future-water-supply/)

---

## Task 

You are tasked with developing and testing a rapid protocol* to efficiently identify and characterise seep wetland vegetation communities on Potberg.

.footnote[*This does not mean that your study methods should be rapid, but rather that they help identify a rapid method.]

---

# Deliverable

A brief research report in the format of a Research Article in the journal [**_Biology Letters_**](https://royalsocietypublishing.org/rsbl/for-authors).

- 2,500 words maximum, including references.
- Standard journal paper format: Title, Abstract, Introduction, Methods, Results (with figures and tables), Discussion, References
- Consider relevant references from the lectures...
- Clearly state your research question(s) and hypothesis(es).
- Present your results in a way that is clear and easy to interpret.
- Discuss your results in the context of your hypothesis and the literature.
- Feel free to highlight the shortcomings of your study and what could be done to improve it.
- Conclude with a summary of your findings and their implications.
- More on how to write a paper [**here**](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1xidafYQKbNyvfvBRtj7-NblW6sg_9_h5HJWgtUsgasY/edit?usp=sharing).

## What can you use as indicators?

---

## What is a wetland?

Wetlands are defined by the presence of water at or near the soil surface (which may be seasonal), hydric soils, and specially adapted vegetation (hydrophytes).

--

### What are the indicators of a wetland?

--

- Wetlands tend to have higher soil moisture (or a shallower water table) than the surrounding landscape.

- Wetlands tend to support distinct plant communities relative to the surrounding landscape, often more productive and typically dominated by hydrophytes.

- Wetlands tend to have hydric soils, which are soils that are saturated, flooded, or ponded long enough during the growing season to develop anaerobic conditions in the upper part. A good indicator of this is higher organic matter content (i.e. darker soils).

## Field equipment?

#### Soil moisture?
- The Aston (metal bar) + 5 pound hammer + 5m measuring tape + glove
- Trowel, sealable plastic bags, permanent marker

#### Vegetation?
- Species: 20m measuring tape, large plastic bags, permanent markers, masking tape, smartphone with camera

- Properties: 5m measuring tape, densiometer, clipboard, paper and pen/pencil

#### Soil organic matter?
- See _Soil moisture_ above (can inspect same sample in lab)

#### Site?
- GPS, clipboard, paper and pen/pencil, 50m measuring tape?

---

## Data sheet?

--

- Site name or number
- GPS coords
- Date, Time
- Observer(s)
- Water table depth (cm)
- Soil sample collected (Y/N)
- Site photos collected (Y/N, camera/owner, numbers/timestamp)
- Vegetation plot established (Y/N)
- Vegetation height (m)
- Vegetation cover (%)
- Densiometer reading
- Species recorded (list)
- Notes

## Results: The Dataset

```{r echo = F, fig.align = 'center', out.height = '60%', warning=F, messages=F}
library(tidyverse)
library(readxl)
library(sf)
library(terra)
library(mapview)
library(rinat)

set.seed(1234) #So I get the same results each time

d1 = read_xlsx("prac/2026/wetlands_BIO3018F_2026 complete.xlsx", sheet = "Sheet1")

d1 = d1 %>% mutate(MoistureFraction = 1 - `Dry mass (g)`/`Wet mass (g)`)

d1 %>% select(!c(Habitat,Pair)) %>%
  kable("html") %>% 
  kable_styling("striped", full_width = F) %>%
  scroll_box(width = "100%", height = "500px")
 
```

---

## Results: Site level

```{r echo = F, fig.align = 'center'}

# Plot site-level indicators of wetness (soil moisture, bare ground, vegetation height)
d1 %>% filter(Species == "Soil") %>%
  rename("Soil Moisture Fraction" = MoistureFraction, 
         "Vegetation Height (m)" = `Veg Height (m)`) %>%
  select(Site, `Site Number`, `Soil Moisture Fraction`, `Bare Ground (%)`, `Vegetation Height (m)`) %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = c(`Soil Moisture Fraction`, `Bare Ground (%)`, `Vegetation Height (m)`), names_to = "Variable", values_to = "Value") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = `Site Number`, y = Value, fill = Site)) +
  geom_col(outlier.shape = NA, position = "dodge") +
  facet_wrap(~Variable, scales = "free_y")
```
While we estimated bare ground at the wet sites, it was always zero, so these bars are not visible. 

.footnote[Why no bare ground at the dry sample at site E?]

---

## Results: Vegetation Community

```{r echo = F, fig.align = 'center'}
# Plot community-level indicators of wetness (leaf moisture fraction) for all species across sites
d1 %>% filter(Species != "Soil") %>% 
  rename("Leaf Moisture Fraction" = MoistureFraction) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = `Site Number`, y = `Leaf Moisture Fraction`, colour = Site)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_point()
```

Leaf moisture fraction (1 - dry mass/wet mass) for all plant species collected across sites. Each boxplot summarises the distribution of leaf moisture fraction for all species collected at each site, and the points show the values for each individual plant sampled.

---

## Results: Species Level

```{r echo = F, fig.align = 'center'}

# Plot species-level indicators of wetness (leaf moisture fraction) for all species that occur in both wet and dry sites
 d1 %>% group_by(Species) %>%
  rename("Leaf Moisture Fraction" = MoistureFraction) %>%
  filter(Species != "Soil", n_distinct(Site) >= 2) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = Species, y = `Leaf Moisture Fraction`, colour = Site)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_point() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, vjust = 1))
```

Leaf moisture fraction (1 - dry mass/wet mass) for all plant species that occur in both wet and dry sites. Each boxplot summarises the distribution of leaf moisture fraction for each species across sites, and the points show the values for each individual plant sampled.

---

## What have we learned so far?

--

It seems that...

- Wet sites have higher soil moisture content than dry sites
- Wet sites tend to have plants with higher leaf moisture content than dry sites
- Some species occur only in wet sites, some only in dry sites, and some in both
- Within species, individuals in wet sites tend to have higher leaf moisture content than in dry sites

<br>

...but we haven't done any statistics, so we can't be sure that these patterns are real and not just due to random variation in our small sample size. I'll leave it up to you to work this bit out...

## Plant distributions as indicators?

```{r echo = F}

#Call the data directly from iNat
bl <- get_inat_obs(taxon_name = "Berzelia lanuginosa",
                   bounds = c(-34.426285, 20.512737, -34.348832, 20.776036),
                   maxresults = 1000) %>%
            filter(positional_accuracy<46 &
                latitude<0 &
                !is.na(latitude) &
                captive_cultivated == "false" &
                quality_grade == "research")

#Make the dataframe a spatial object of class = "sf"
bl <- st_as_sf(bl, coords = c("longitude", "latitude"), crs = 4326)

mapview::mapview(bl, zcol = "positional_accuracy", legend = FALSE)

```

.footnote[iNaturalist records of the occurrence of the vlei kolkol (_Berzelia lanuginosa_) in De Hoop Nature Reserve. It is a good indicator of wet environments, but occurs only in a few locations on Potberg.]

## Problem

One needs to "ground-truth" remote sensing data with on-the-ground surveys to be sure that you are mapping wetlands and not other features.

---

### Do our sites match up with our remotely sensed moisture index?

#### [Moisture Index (MI)](https://custom-scripts.sentinel-hub.com/custom-scripts/sentinel-2/msi/)
```{r echo = F}
# Read in Sentinel moisture indices
ndmi <- rast("prac/2026/NDMI_custom.tiff")[[1]] # ranges 0 to 1
mi <- rast("prac/2026/MI_custom.tiff")[[1]]/255*3 # rescale to 0-3 

# Get site coordinates and convert to spatial object
sites_sf <- d1 %>% select(`Site Number`, Site, Latitude, Longitude) %>% 
  unique() %>% 
  st_as_sf(coords = c("Longitude", "Latitude"), crs = 4326)

# Plot MI and add points for the site locations
mapview(mi) + mapview(sites_sf, label = sites_sf$`Site Number`)
```

.footnote[MI is calculated by dividing the SWIR by the NIR bands of Sentinel 2 data, and is negatively correlated with moisture.]

---

### Do our sites match up with normalised difference moisture index?

#### [Normalised Difference Moisture Index (NDMI)](https://custom-scripts.sentinel-hub.com/custom-scripts/sentinel-2/ndmi/)
```{r echo = F}
# Plot NDMI and add points for the site locations
mapview(ndmi) + mapview(sites_sf, label = sites_sf$`Site Number`)
```

.footnote[NDMI is the normalised difference of the NIR and SWIR bands of Sentinel 2 data, and is positively correlated with moisture.]

---

### Do our sites match up with our remotely sensed moisture indices?

```{r echo = F}
# Extract NDMI and MI values at the site locations
sites_sf <- sites_sf %>% mutate(NDMI = terra::extract(ndmi, sites_sf)[,2],
                      MI = terra::extract(mi, sites_sf)[,2])

# Plot NDMI and MI at the site locations
sites_sf %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = c(`NDMI`, `MI`), names_to = "Variable", values_to = "Value") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = `Site Number`, y = Value, fill = Site)) +
  geom_col(outlier.shape = NA, position = "dodge") +
  facet_wrap(~Variable, scales = "free_y")
```

## Traits from remote sensing?

```{r echo = F}
# Extract leaf water content at the site locations
sites_sf <- sites_sf %>% mutate(`Leaf Water Content` = terra::extract(wat, sites_sf, method = "bilinear")[,2])

# Plot leaf water content at the site locations
sites_sf %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = `Site Number`, y = `Leaf Water Content`, fill = Site)) +
  geom_col(outlier.shape = NA, position = "dodge")
```

.footnote[Like I said... preliminary...]

---

## Traits from remote sensing?

### What about the leaf water content estimates for our Berzelia localities?

```{r echo = F}
# Extract estimates for our Berzelia localities
berz <- terra::extract(wat[[1]], bl)

# Generate background points (e.g., 100 points)
bg_pts <- spatSample(wat[[1]], size=100, "random", as.points=TRUE)
bg_vals <- terra::extract(wat[[1]], bg_pts)

# Plot comparison as a density plot
tibble(Target = factor(c(rep("Berzelia", nrow(berz)), rep("Background", nrow(bg_vals)))),
  `Leaf Water Content` = rbind(berz,bg_vals)[,2]) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = `Leaf Water Content`, fill = Target)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.5) +
  labs(x = "Estimated Leaf Water Content", fill = "Target") +
  theme_minimal()
```
